doubts: Piemonte appellations: No official per-denomination table of hectares (Regione Piemonte schedario or Vignaioli Piemontesi) could be read: regione.piemonte.it statistics pages and vignaioli.it PDFs were blocked or held no such table. Most vine_area_ha values come from Italian Wine Central (2021, secondary, basis not stated).

Piemonte appellations: For Barolo, Barbaresco, Dogliani, Dolcetto di Diano d'Alba, Barbera d'Alba, Nebbiolo d'Alba, Dolcetto d'Alba and Langhe, the hectares are Consorzio figures cited by Vertdevin (Jan 2025) without a reference year. They are 10 to 80% higher than Italian Wine Central 2021 figures, which suggests registered versus claimed area. Check against the Consorzio before publishing.

Piemonte appellations: Barbera d'Asti uses an official figure (5,125 ha suitable in the schedario, 2022, Regione Piemonte DD 1190/2023). Italian Wine Central gives 3,560 ha for 2021, probably claimed area.

Piemonte appellations: Region vineyard area differs by source: 44,471 ha provisional 2024 (Regione Piemonte / Vignaioli Piemontesi), 43,670 ha DO-suitable 2024 (Regione Piemonte), 41,699 ha 2024 (Anagrafe Agricola via David Way), 39,400 ha 2024 (ISTAT), 43,536 ha 2022 (Italian Wine Central). A later Way article gives about 42,000 ha for 2026 and different 2024 variety figures (Barbera 10,762, Moscato 10,426, Nebbiolo 7,313, Dolcetto 3,308) than his 2025 article used here.

Piemonte appellations: Grape shares are computed from secondary data (David Way) against his own total; Italian Wine Central gives 2022 shares of Barbera 31%, Moscato 22%, Dolcetto 13%, Nebbiolo 10%, which look outdated.

Piemonte appellations: Canelli became a separate DOCG in 2023 (Moscato Bianco; Riserva 30 months, 20 in bottle) but it is not among the 59 atlas PDOs, so it has no record here. Piedmont is now counted as 19 DOCG and 41 DOC; the 59 atlas PDOs are 18 DOCG and 41 DOC.
Piemonte appellations: Terre Alfieri is DOCG since 2020 per Italian Wine Central; DOCG year not checked against the Gazzetta Ufficiale.

Piemonte appellations: Nizza has doc_year null: it was a subzone of Barbera d'Asti Superiore (DOC) from 2000 before the 2014 DOCG. Dogliani docg_year 2005 is the Dogliani Superiore DOCG; the DOCG was later extended to all Dogliani. Dolcetto di Ovada Superiore doc_year 1972 is the year of the Dolcetto di Ovada DOC.

Piemonte appellations: Ageing rules and recognition years come from Italian Wine Central and Wine with Seth, not from the disciplinari themselves (the MASAF, eAmbrosia and Regione Piemonte disciplinare files were blocked). The Asti DOCG specification was amended in 2026 (EU OJ 31 July 2026); the content of the change was not checked.

Piemonte appellations: Dogliani: the 21 commune names given as subzones are menzioni geografiche aggiuntive per Italian Wine Central; the other vineyard MeGA (about 55) are not listed. Diano d'Alba: 75 sorì / MeGA count only.
Piemonte appellations: Colli Tortonesi: the name Derthona is used by producers for Timorasso; its legal status in the disciplinare was not checked.
Piemonte appellations: Loazzolo: Italian Wine Central gives 51 ha but Federdoc gives only 1.06 ha declared in 2016; the larger figure probably counts all Moscato eligible for the DOC.
Piemonte appellations: Alta Langa hectares (455 ha, 2023) are fast growing; Winemag.it (Jan 2023) suggested about 597 ha after the 2023 to 2025 plan.

Piemonte appellations: Federdoc ed. 2017 gives 2016 declared hectares for all 59 denominations (e.g. Barolo 1,747.62, Barbaresco 670.93, Asti 7,770.11, Langhe 1,614.51, Piemonte 3,192.51, region total 28,799.87); it was used only as a cross check.

Piemonte appellations: Small DOCs with 2021 Italian Wine Central figures of 10 ha or less (Alba, Calosso, Carema, Cisterna d'Asti, Colline Saluzzesi, Collina Torinese, Fara, Gabiano, Rubino di Cantavenna, Sizzano, Strevi, Valsusa) carry large relative uncertainty.

Langhe and Roero crus: Barolo MGA list: 170 names from art. 8 of the disciplinare (AIS consolidated text to DM 17.04.2015) plus 11 'del comune di' mentions = 181. The Allegato with MGA boundaries is not in the published disciplinare text, so the MGA to commune mapping comes from the Enoteca Regionale del Barolo 'Locate MGAs' page; it matched all 170 names.

Langhe and Roero crus: Barolo MGA crossing communes (Enoteca Regionale del Barolo): Brunate, Cerequio and Fossati (Barolo and La Morra), Bussia (Monforte d'Alba and Barolo), Ravera (Novello and Barolo), Rocche di Castiglione (Castiglione Falletto and Monforte d'Alba), Sorano (Serralunga d'Alba and Diano d'Alba). Some secondary sources place Bussia in Monforte only. Bricco San Biagio is in La Morra only per the Enoteca; it does not span communes.

Langhe and Roero crus: Barolo name spellings follow the AIS text of art. 8: 'Bergeisa' (Enoteca writes Bergesia), 'Galina', 'Vignarionda' (often written Vigna Rionda), 'Cerviano-Merli', and alternatives joined by 'o' such as 'Cannubi Boschis o Cannubi'. The AIS text spells the Monforte commune mention 'Manforte d'Alba', an evident typo; the key uses Monforte d'Alba. 'Gallaretto' and 'Garretti' appear run together in one text extraction; they are two MGA (Diano d'Alba and Grinzane Cavour).
Langhe and Roero crus: Alba is not in the Barolo zone under art. 3 of the Barolo disciplinare (eleven communes, Alba not among them). Alba is only in the Barbaresco zone, for San Rocco Seno d'Elvio.

Langhe and Roero crus: Barbaresco: 66 MGA from art. 7 of the disciplinare; commune mapping from the Enoteca Regionale del Barbaresco. Meruzzano, Montersino and Rizzi lie in both Treiso and Alba (San Rocco Seno d'Elvio). The AIS text writes accented names with apostrophes (Paje', Rabaja', Pajore'); accented forms Pajè, Rabajà, Pajorè are used. 'Bernadot' follows the disciplinare; the Enoteca writes Bernardot.

Langhe and Roero crus: Roero count: Allegato 2A lists 18 communes (Castellinaldo d'Alba is in the zone but has no commune-level mention) and Allegato 2B 134 frazioni/localita, if 'Tavolato Colla' in the AIS text is read as two names (Tavoleto in Sommariva Perno, Colla in Vezza d'Alba, as the parcel tables show). That is 152 entries. Three 2B names occur twice in different communes (Roncaglie, San Michele, Madonna delle Grazie), so 149 distinct names. The Consorzio said 135 MGA (19 communal) at launch in 2017 and Strada del Barolo says 134; the list was later extended, probably with Reg. UE 2022/2044.

Langhe and Roero crus: Roero MGA to commune mapping: list order in Allegato 2B groups names by commune; extra communes come from the cadastral parcel tables as read by text extraction. Treat cross-commune assignments as provisional. Spelling clashes between the name list and the parcel tables: Precetto/Pecetto (Canale), San Silverio/San Siverio (Priocca), Serra Zanni/Serra Zoanni (Castellinaldo d'Alba), Bricco di Piovesi/Piobesi (Piobesi d'Alba), Tavolato/Tavoleto. Castellinaldo parcel rows labelled 'Roncaglia' have no matching name in the list and were left out. 'Cortine' sits in the Castagnito block of the list, but its parcel rows read under Guarene; it is put in both. 'Corso' (Montà block) has no parcel rows in the extracted text.
Langhe and Roero crus: Roero names: trailing apostrophes in the AIS text were turned into accents (Casà, Lamontà, Trinità, S.S. Trinità).

Langhe and Roero crus: vine_area_ha by commune is the 2010 Albo Vigneti of the Camera di Commercio di Cuneo, the latest official per-commune split found. Totals 2010: Barolo 1,886.90 ha, Barbaresco 685.73 ha, Roero 195.80 ha plus Roero Arneis 694.37 ha. Areas have grown since: Regione Piemonte DD 207/2026 and 206/2026 call 22 ha and 7 ha a 1% yearly increase, which implies about 2,200 ha of Barolo and 700 ha of Barbaresco. For Barbaresco and Roero the newer undated figures of the Enoteca Regionale del Barbaresco (763.19 ha total) and the Consorzio Tutela Roero are given in vine_area_alt.

Langhe and Roero crus: No official vine_area_ha was found for individual MGA. The Consorzio Barolo Barbaresco site (langhevini.it) blocks automated reading and Masnaghetti's Enogea 360 pages could not be fetched. Figures from producers (Produttori del Barbaresco list their members' hectares per cru, not the MGA total) and from WineWithSeth were not used as MGA areas.

Langhe and Roero crus: MGA descriptions (aspect, altitude, soils, owners) come from producer pages (Vietti, Produttori del Barbaresco) and WineWithSeth, all secondary sources. Commune descriptions for Barolo use Wine Scholar Guild and WineWithSeth; for Barbaresco the Enoteca Regionale del Barbaresco; for Roero the Consorzio Tutela Roero.

Langhe and Roero crus: partial_communes on MGA records lists every commune the MGA touches, since an MGA never covers a whole commune. On menzione comunale records it lists the commune only when the commune is partly outside the DOCG zone.

Toscana: Per-appellation hectares: official recent figures (ARTEA schedario at 31 July 2024) were found only for the 10 largest DOP (Chianti, Chianti Classico, Brunello, Rosso di Montalcino, Vino Nobile, Rosso di Montepulciano, Morellino, Vernaccia, Bolgheri red and white). All other DOC and the small DOCG use Italian Wine Central figures for 2021 or 2022, a secondary source that does not name its own source. ARTEA 2013 harvest figures are given in vine_area_src where they help.

Toscana: ARTEA publishes the full claimable register per denomination as open data (dati.toscana.it, 'ARTEA Albi vigneti rivendicabili dal 2015', CSV per year up to 2025). The file could not be downloaded here (host blocked), so per-DOC totals were not computed. Summing area_mq by 'albo' in albivignetirivendicabili2025.csv would give official 2025 hectares for every DOC, DOCG and Chianti sottozona.

Toscana: ARTEA claimable area, Consorzio figures and IWC figures measure different things (registered claimable, planted, claimed at harvest). Vino Nobile: ARTEA 2024 1,389 ha vs Consorzio 1,102 ha. Rosso di Montepulciano: 584 vs 214 ha. Rosso di Montalcino: ARTEA 529 ha vs Consorzio 860 ha. Chianti: 17,054 vs 15,500 ha. Chianti Classico: 7,870 vs 7,200 ha.
Toscana: Bolgheri hectares use the Consorzio figure (1,379 ha, year not stated, page current in 2026). ARTEA lists 1,447 ha red and 201 ha white claimable at 31 July 2024; these may overlap.

Toscana: Chianti sottozone hectares are only available from ARTEA 2013 harvest declarations (official but 13 years old). Recent per-sottozona figures were not found. Wikipedia gives 2006 figures and Rufina sources give 750 to 850 ha registered (secondary, no year).

Toscana: Chianti sottozone communes come from the Art. 3 text as quoted by Lavinium, which lists each set 'in tutto o in parte' without saying which communes are partial. partial_communes is filled only where it is certain: communes shared with Chianti Classico, and Montespertoli in Colli Fiorentini. Pelago and Pontassieve appear in both Colli Fiorentini and Rufina, and Vinci and Capraia e Limite in both Montalbano and Terre di Vinci; how they are split was not confirmed. Old commune names were mapped to current ISTAT names: Figline Val d'Arno and Incisa to Figline e Incisa Valdarno; Lastra to Lastra a Signa; Barberino Val d'Elsa and Tavarnelle Val di Pesa to Barberino Tavarnelle; Castelfranco di Sopra and Pian di Sco to Castelfranco Piandiscò; Laterina and Pergine Valdarno to Laterina Pergine Valdarno; Casciana Terme and Lari to Casciana Terme Lari; Crespina to Crespina Lorenzana.

Toscana: Chianti sottozone lists differ by source. it.wikipedia adds Firenze to Colli Fiorentini (Lavinium has Signa instead). it.wikipedia adds Serravalle Pistoiese, Carmignano, Poggio a Caiano and Cerreto Guidi to Montalbano. Assovini gives the same 14 Colli Aretini communes. A check against the current disciplinare on the MASAF site is advised.

Toscana: The 2026 Chianti amendment (rosato, Sangiovese minimum 60%, Terre di Vinci sottozona) was reported as published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale by Gambero Rosso on 16 June 2026. The GU text itself was not read. The Terre di Vinci commune list (Vinci, Cerreto Guidi, Fucecchio, Capraia e Limite) comes from wein.plus at the regional approval stage.

Toscana: Chianti Classico communes: there are 8 communes under current ISTAT names. The historic count of 9 predates the 2019 merger of Barberino Val d'Elsa and Tavarnelle Val di Pesa into Barberino Tavarnelle. The Production Code (Art. 9) names only four partial communes and not Poggibonsi, but the Consorzio site and the San Donato in Poggio UGA text include part of Poggibonsi.

Toscana: UGA hectares: the Consorzio UGA pages give vineyard hectares for San Casciano, Greve, Montefioralle, Vagliagli, Castelnuovo Berardenga and San Donato in Poggio. Castellina, Gaiole, Lamole, Panzano and Radda come from Wine Folly (secondary), which matches the Consorzio wherever both give a figure. No year is stated for these hectares.
Toscana: UGA approval: the Consorzio assembly approved the UGA in June 2021. Decanter dates official publication in the Gazzetta Ufficiale to 1 July 2023. The ministerial decree itself was not read.

Toscana: Pievi of Vino Nobile: the 12 names and boundaries come from DM 21 Jan 2025 (GU n. 29, 5 Feb 2025). No hectares per Pieve were found. Soil and altitude notes are by group, from Tenute del Cerro, a producer site. The Consorzio 2024 press kit lists 14 draft names, which differ from the final decree.

Toscana: Pieve coordinates: no point coordinates were found for Cerliana (La Ciarliana), Sant'Ilario or Valardegna. Le Grazie and San Biagio use bus stops of those names from a Siena GTFS feed, so they are approximate. The other villages use OpenStreetMap place nodes or Who's On First.

Toscana: UGA village coordinates come from OpenStreetMap place nodes in a Tuscany extract on GitHub (direct OSM, Wikipedia and Wikidata access was blocked here). They agree within about 150 m with en.wikipedia (Montefioralle, Vagliagli, Castellina) and GeoNames (Lamole, Panzano) where checked.

Toscana: Other official sub-zones: Bolgheri Sassicaia is its own DOC, not a sub-zone. Montalcino has no official sub-zones. Terraelectae in Chianti Rufina is a private producer label, not part of the disciplinare. The Valdarno di Sopra sub-zones Pietraviva and Pratomagno were voted for abolition in Dec 2023; whether the decree is in force was not confirmed, so they are not listed. The Vin Santo del Chianti DOC uses the same seven sottozone names as Chianti.

Toscana: DOCG count: 11 DOCG and 41 DOC (Toscana Promozione, Jan 2026). The atlas has 51 Tuscan PDOs; the missing one is Colli di Luni, which Tuscany shares with Liguria. Orcia aims for DOCG status but was not upgraded as of the sources read.

Toscana: doc_year is left null for Suvereto and Val di Cornia Rosso. Both were sub-zones of the Val di Cornia DOC (1989) before their 2011 DOCG, but the year each sub-zone was added was not confirmed. For Chianti Classico, doc_year 1967 and docg_year 1984 refer to its time as part of Chianti; it became a separate DOCG in 1996.
Toscana: Maremma toscana, Colli dell'Etruria Centrale and Vin Santo del Chianti are tagged deep_level 'regional' as wide umbrella DOC.

region.vine_area_src: Provisional vineyard area from 2024 harvest declarations, given at the presentation of L'Annata Vitivinicola in Piemonte 2024 (Regione Piemonte and Vignaioli Piemontesi), reported by Gazzetta d'Alba (Jan 2025); 44,285 ha in 2023. Other 2024 figures: 43,670 ha suitable for DO wine and 36,193 ha claimed for DO wine (Regione Piemonte data sheet); 39,400 ha (ISTAT, via inumeridelvino).
region.grape_share_note: Percent of 41,699 ha, the 2024 total in the Regione Piemonte vineyard register (Anagrafe Agricola) as published by David Way (Winefriend, first in Decanter, Apr 2025): Barbera 10,099 ha, Moscato Bianco 9,833, Nebbiolo 6,835, Dolcetto 3,115, Cortese 2,680, Arneis 1,346, Chardonnay 1,286, Pinot Nero 735, Timorasso 439, Erbaluce 322. Shares computed by us. Secondary source. White varieties were about 40% of plantings in 2024, against 33% in 2008.
region.atlas_note: Piedmont has about 44,000 ha of vines, mostly on the hills of the provinces of Cuneo, Asti and Alessandria south of the Po, with smaller areas in the north around Novara, Vercelli, Biella and Turin. Barbera and Moscato Bianco are the most planted grapes, followed by Nebbiolo, which has grown by about two thirds since 2008 while Dolcetto has halved. The region has 19 DOCG and 41 DOC and no IGT, and almost all of its wine is sold as DO wine. Vineyard area fell sharply in 2025 and 2026 as growers grubbed up vines.

Alta Langa.atlas_note: Alta Langa is a traditional method sparkling wine DOCG on the high hills of the Langhe, Roero and Monferrato, in the provinces of Cuneo, Asti and Alessandria. It is made from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay. Only vintage dated wines are allowed. The area under vine has grown fast since the DOCG was granted.

Asti.atlas_note: Asti DOCG covers the Moscato Bianco hills of the provinces of Asti, Cuneo and Alessandria, in 51 communes. It has two main wines: Asti (Asti Spumante), a fully sparkling sweet wine, and Moscato d'Asti, a lightly sparkling wine with low alcohol. It is the largest DOCG in Piedmont by volume. A Metodo Classico and late harvest versions are also allowed.

Barbaresco.atlas_note: Barbaresco is a 100% Nebbiolo DOCG north east of Alba, in the communes of Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso and the San Rocco Seno d'Elvio part of Alba. Its slopes run down to the Tanaro. The wines are often seen as more approachable young than Barolo, with a shorter minimum ageing. Vineyard names are regulated as MGA.

Barbera del Monferrato Superiore.atlas_note: This DOCG is the aged Superiore version of Barbera del Monferrato, from the hills of the Monferrato in the provinces of Alessandria and Asti. It is at least 85% Barbera with small amounts of Freisa, Grignolino or Dolcetto. Volumes are very small.

Barolo.vine_area_src: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures, as cited by Vertdevin (29 Jan 2025); reference year not stated, probably area registered in the schedario (secondary citation). Italian Wine Central gives 2,057 ha for 2021.
Barolo.atlas_note: Barolo is a 100% Nebbiolo DOCG south west of Alba, in 11 communes of the Langhe. Barolo, Castiglione Falletto and Serralunga d'Alba lie wholly inside the zone; La Morra, Monforte d'Alba, Verduno, Novello, Grinzane Cavour, Diano d'Alba, Cherasco and Roddi are partly inside. Its tannic, long lived wines need at least 38 months of ageing. Vineyard names are regulated as MGA.
rules: 181 menzioni geografiche aggiuntive, 11 of them commune names (listed by another agent)
22 ha a year, 0.5 ha per farm (Regione Piemonte bandi 2023 to 2026)
refs: Vertdevin, Grandi Langhe 2025 (Consorzio Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures)

items: Altenasso o Garblet Suè o Garbelletto Superiore
Mariondino o Monriondino o Bricco Moriondino
notes: Bricco San Biagio
MGA in the commune of La Morra.
Brunate
MGA across La Morra and Barolo. About 230 to 405 m, facing south to southeast, on Tortonian Sant'Agata marls rich in silt.
Bussia

MGA across Monforte d'Alba and a small part of Barolo. One of the largest MGA of Barolo, a broad amphitheatre of slopes with many aspects; historic names such as Bussia Soprana, Bussia Sottana, Romirasco and Cicala lie inside it.
Cannubi

MGA in the commune of Barolo, on the long Cannubi hill north of the village. Tortonian and Serravallian marls meet here. Under art. 8 the neighbouring MGA Cannubi Boschis, Cannubi Muscatel, Cannubi San Lorenzo and Cannubi Valletta may also be labelled Cannubi.
Cerequio
MGA across La Morra and Barolo, next to Brunate. About 290 to 400 m on Tortonian Sant'Agata marls, with one face toward Brunate and the other south to southeast.
Falletto
MGA in the commune of Serralunga d'Alba. Steep southwest facing slopes in an amphitheatre; farmed by Bruno Giacosa since 1982.
Fossati
MGA across Barolo and La Morra, in the west of the zone.
Francia
MGA in the commune of Serralunga d'Alba, at the south end of the commune. Owned by Giacomo Conterno since 1974.
Ginestra
MGA in the commune of Monforte d'Alba, facing southeast toward Serralunga. Limestone-rich soils.
La Serra
MGA in the commune of La Morra, near the top of the village hill at about 370 to 450 m.
Lazzarito
MGA in the commune of Serralunga d'Alba. About 260 to 390 m on Serravallian Lequio formation soils.
Monprivato
MGA in the commune of Castiglione Falletto. An amphitheatre facing south-southwest, about 240 to 330 m. Most of it is farmed by Giuseppe Mascarello e Figlio.
Monvigliero
MGA in the commune of Verduno. About 220 to 310 m, facing southeast to southwest, on laminated Tortonian Sant'Agata marls.
Ravera
MGA across Novello and Barolo. About 300 to 480 m, mainly east facing, on laminated Tortonian Sant'Agata marls.
Rocche dell'Annunziata
MGA in the commune of La Morra, in the Annunziata area. It is one of the best known crus of La Morra.
Rocche di Castiglione
MGA across Castiglione Falletto and Monforte d'Alba. A steep scarp at about 300 to 350 m, mainly southeast facing, on sandy Sant'Agata marls over Diano sandstone.
Sorano
MGA across Serralunga d'Alba and Diano d'Alba, at the northeast end of the Serralunga ridge. Faces southeast to south-southwest on calcareous-clay Sant'Agata marls.
Vignarionda
MGA in the commune of Serralunga d'Alba, also written Vigna Rionda. South to southwest facing, at about 300 to 330 m on the Lequio formation; shared by many producers.
Villero
MGA in the commune of Castiglione Falletto, on the east side of its ridge. About 230 to 350 m, facing west to southwest, on sandy Sant'Agata marls.

Brachetto d'Acqui / Acqui.atlas_note: Brachetto d'Acqui is a sweet, aromatic red DOCG from Brachetto grown around Acqui Terme, in 26 communes of the provinces of Alessandria and Asti. Most of it is sparkling or lightly sparkling and low in alcohol. A passito and a drier rose labelled Acqui are also made.
rules: about 9 months; release from 1 October after harvest

Dogliani.vine_area_src: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures, as cited by Vertdevin (29 Jan 2025); reference year not stated, probably area registered in the schedario (secondary citation). Italian Wine Central gives 449 ha for 2021.
Dogliani.atlas_note: Dogliani is a 100% Dolcetto DOCG in the southern Langhe around the town of Dogliani, in 21 communes of the province of Cuneo. It was the DOC Dolcetto di Dogliani from 1974. The DOCG was first given to the Superiore in 2005 and later extended to the whole denomination. It is the most structured Dolcetto of Piedmont.
rules: 12 months (Italian Wine Central; Superiore rule not checked)
76 menzioni geografiche aggiuntive, including the 21 commune names (Italian Wine Central)

Dolcetto di Diano d'Alba / Diano d'Alba.vine_area_src: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures, as cited by Vertdevin (29 Jan 2025); reference year not stated, probably area registered in the schedario (secondary citation). Italian Wine Central gives 115 ha for 2021.
Dolcetto di Diano d'Alba / Diano d'Alba.atlas_note: This 100% Dolcetto DOCG covers only the commune of Diano d'Alba, on the ridge between the Barolo zone and Alba. Its vineyard sites are recognised as sorì. A Superiore needs about 10 months of ageing.
rules: about 10 months; release from 1 September after harvest
refs: Vertdevin, Grandi Langhe 2025 (Consorzio Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures)

Dolcetto di Ovada Superiore / Ovada.atlas_note: Ovada DOCG is the aged Superiore version of Dolcetto from the hills around Ovada, in 22 communes in the south of the province of Alessandria. It was part of the Dolcetto di Ovada DOC, recognised in 1972, until the DOCG of 2008. Production is very small.
rules: 12 months; release from 1 November after harvest

Italian Wine Central, Dolcetto di Ovada DOC

Erbaluce di Caluso / Caluso.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed). Winefriend (David Way, from Regione Piemonte register data) gives 322 ha of Erbaluce in Piedmont in 2024, across several DOCs.
Erbaluce di Caluso / Caluso.atlas_note: Erbaluce di Caluso is a white DOCG from the Erbaluce grape, grown on the morainic hills of the Canavese around Caluso, north of Turin. It is made as a dry still white, a traditional method sparkling wine and a passito. The passito has long minimum ageing.
rules: traditional method, at least 15 months on the lees
refs: Italian Wine Central, Erbaluce di Caluso / Caluso DOCG

Gattinara.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed). David Way (Northern Piemonte Report 2026) gives around 90 ha in production.
Gattinara.atlas_note: Gattinara is a Nebbiolo based DOCG from the single commune of Gattinara in the province of Vercelli, on the left bank of the Sesia. The vineyards lie on volcanic, acid soils at the foot of the Alps. It needs long ageing in wood.
rules: at least 90% Nebbiolo (Spanna); up to 10% Uva Rara and up to 4% Vespolina

Gavi / Cortese di Gavi.vine_area_src: Consorzio Tutela del Gavi figure (about 1,600 ha) reported by The Buyer, Oct 2024. Winefriend (David Way, from Regione Piemonte register data) gives 1,594 ha of Cortese for Gavi; Italian Wine Central gives 1,609 ha for 2021.
Gavi / Cortese di Gavi.atlas_note: Gavi is a white DOCG of 100% Cortese from 11 communes in the south east of the province of Alessandria, close to Liguria. It makes still, frizzante and sparkling wines. Wines from one commune may carry its name as "del comune di"; only Gavi from the commune of Gavi itself may use that commune name on the label. Most of the wine is exported.
rules: 1 year, of which 6 months in bottle
Charmat at least 6 months on the lees; metodo classico at least 9 months
2 years, of which 18 months on the lees
"del comune di" plus commune name allowed for tranquillo, frizzante and spumante; not for Riserva
refs: Italian Wine Central, Gavi / Cortese di Gavi DOCG
The Buyer, Consorzio reveals first insights from Gavi DOCG 2024 vintage
Wine with Seth, Gavi / Cortese di Gavi DOCG

Ghemme.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Ghemme.atlas_note: Ghemme is a Nebbiolo based DOCG from Ghemme and Romagnano Sesia in the province of Novara, on the right bank of the Sesia facing Gattinara. The vineyards lie on old glacial moraine. It needs long ageing in wood.
rules: at least 85% Nebbiolo (Spanna); up to 15% Vespolina and/or Uva Rara

Nizza.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Nizza.atlas_note: Nizza is a 100% Barbera DOCG from 18 communes around Nizza Monferrato in the province of Asti. It began in 2000 as a subzone of Barbera d'Asti Superiore and became a separate DOCG in 2014. Its own consortium was recognised in June 2026. About 1.09 million bottles were sold in 2024.
rules: vineyard name allowed, same ageing as Nizza or Nizza Riserva
refs: Michele Chiarlo, The Consorzio del Nizza DOCG is officially recognized

Roero.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed). Winefriend (David Way, from Regione Piemonte register data) gives 922 ha of Arneis for Roero.
Roero.atlas_note: Roero lies on the left bank of the Tanaro, north of Alba, in 19 communes of the province of Cuneo. Its sandy soils give a white from Arneis (Roero Arneis) and a red from Nebbiolo (Roero). The white is by far the larger part of production. Vineyard names are regulated as MGA.
rules: at least 95% Nebbiolo; 20 months, of which 6 in wood
153 menzioni geografiche aggiuntive, 19 of them commune names (listed by another agent)
Roero Arneis 40 ha in 2024; Roero 25 ha in 2026 (Regione Piemonte bandi)

Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2022 vineyard area (secondary source; basis not stated). Winefriend (David Way, register data) gives 214 ha of Ruchè in Piedmont in 2024.
Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato.atlas_note: Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato is a red DOCG from the aromatic Ruchè grape, grown in Castagnole Monferrato and six nearby communes in the province of Asti. The wine is perfumed, with floral and spice notes. It is one of the smallest DOCGs of Piedmont.
rules: at least 90% Ruchè; up to 10% Barbera and/or Brachetto
at least 2 years, of which 1 in wood

Alba.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Alba.atlas_note: Alba DOC covers the hills around Alba in the Langhe and Roero. It is a red blend of Nebbiolo with Barbera. Production is very small.

Albugnano.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Albugnano.atlas_note: Albugnano is a small Nebbiolo DOC in four communes of the northern Asti hills, near Castelnuovo Don Bosco. It makes red and rosato wines.
rules: 1 year, of which 6 months in wood

Barbera d'Alba.vine_area_src: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures, as cited by Vertdevin (29 Jan 2025); reference year not stated, probably area registered in the schedario (secondary citation). Italian Wine Central gives 1,296 ha for 2021.
Barbera d'Alba.atlas_note: Barbera d'Alba covers the Barbera vineyards of the Langhe and Roero around Alba. It is the main everyday red of the Alba area alongside Dolcetto. The Castellinaldo subzone was added in 2021.
rules: at least 85% Barbera; up to 15% Nebbiolo
14 months, of which 6 in wood and 3 in bottle
refs: Italian Wine Central, Barbera d'Alba DOC
Vertdevin, Grandi Langhe 2025 (Consorzio Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures)

Barbera del Monferrato.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Barbera del Monferrato.atlas_note: Barbera del Monferrato covers a wide area of the Monferrato hills in the provinces of Alessandria and Asti. It is a young, often lightly sparkling Barbera. The aged version is the separate DOCG Barbera del Monferrato Superiore.
rules: at least 85% Barbera; up to 15% Freisa, Grignolino and/or Dolcetto
refs: Italian Wine Central, Barbera del Monferrato DOC

Boca.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Boca.atlas_note: Boca is a small Nebbiolo based DOC in five communes of the hills north of Novara. Its vineyards lie on volcanic soils of an ancient supervolcano. It needs long ageing in wood.
rules: 70 to 90% Nebbiolo (Spanna); 10 to 30% Uva Rara and/or Vespolina

Bramaterra.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Bramaterra.atlas_note: Bramaterra is a Nebbiolo based DOC in seven communes of the provinces of Biella and Vercelli, west of the Sesia. It is a blend with Croatina, Uva Rara and Vespolina.
rules: 50 to 80% Nebbiolo; up to 30% Croatina; up to 20% Uva Rara and/or Vespolina

Calosso.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Calosso.atlas_note: Calosso is a tiny red DOC in three communes of the province of Asti. It is made from the local Gamba Rossa grape, a Barbera related variety.

Canavese.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Canavese.atlas_note: Canavese is a wide DOC for the Canavese area north of Turin, in 105 communes of the provinces of Turin, Biella and Vercelli. It covers whites from Erbaluce and reds and roses from Nebbiolo, Barbera and local grapes. It overlaps the Erbaluce di Caluso and Carema zones.

Carema.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Carema.atlas_note: Carema is a single commune Nebbiolo DOC at the border with the Aosta Valley. The vines grow on stone terraces with pergolas held on stone pillars. It is one of the coolest Nebbiolo sites in Piedmont.

Cisterna d'Asti.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Cisterna d'Asti.atlas_note: Cisterna d'Asti is a small red DOC in 13 communes between Roero and the Asti hills. It is made mainly from Croatina.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Cisterna d'Asti DOC

Colli Tortonesi.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Colli Tortonesi.atlas_note: Colli Tortonesi covers the hills around Tortona in the south east of the province of Alessandria, near Lombardy and Liguria. It is the home of the white Timorasso grape, now its best known wine. Reds come mainly from Barbera. Winefriend gives 397 ha of Timorasso under this DOC.
rules: Barbera only; 20 months, of which 6 in wood
refs: Italian Wine Central, Colli Tortonesi DOC
Winefriend, Is Piemonte becoming a white wine region?

Collina Torinese.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Collina Torinese.atlas_note: Collina Torinese covers the hills east and south of Turin in 28 communes. It makes red and sweet red wines from Barbera, Bonarda, Freisa, Malvasia Nera and Pelaverga (Cari). Volumes are very small.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Collina Torinese DOC

Colline Novaresi.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Colline Novaresi.atlas_note: Colline Novaresi is the wide DOC of the Novara hills in northern Piedmont, in 25 communes. It covers whites from Erbaluce and reds from Nebbiolo, Vespolina, Uva Rara, Croatina and Barbera. It overlaps the Ghemme, Boca, Fara and Sizzano zones.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Colline Novaresi DOC

Colline Saluzzesi.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Colline Saluzzesi.atlas_note: Colline Saluzzesi covers 13 communes around Saluzzo in the province of Cuneo, at the foot of the Alps. It makes red and rose wines from Pelaverga and sweet, sometimes sparkling, reds from Quagliano.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Colline Saluzzesi DOC

Cortese dell'Alto Monferrato.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Cortese dell'Alto Monferrato.atlas_note: Cortese dell'Alto Monferrato covers 86 communes of the southern Monferrato in the provinces of Alessandria and Asti. It makes still and sparkling whites from Cortese. Its zone surrounds the Gavi DOCG.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Cortese dell'Alto Monferrato DOC

Coste della Sesia.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Coste della Sesia.atlas_note: Coste della Sesia is the wide DOC of the hills west of the Sesia in the provinces of Biella and Vercelli, in 16 communes. It covers whites from Erbaluce and reds from Nebbiolo, Croatina and Vespolina. It overlaps Gattinara, Lessona and Bramaterra.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Coste della Sesia DOC

Dolcetto d'Acqui.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Dolcetto d'Acqui.atlas_note: Dolcetto d'Acqui covers 23 communes around Acqui Terme in the province of Alessandria. It is a 100% Dolcetto red.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Dolcetto d'Acqui DOC

Dolcetto d'Alba.vine_area_src: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures, as cited by Vertdevin (29 Jan 2025); reference year not stated, probably area registered in the schedario (secondary citation). Italian Wine Central gives 677 ha for 2021.
Dolcetto d'Alba.atlas_note: Dolcetto d'Alba covers the Dolcetto vineyards of the Langhe and Roero around Alba, in 36 communes. It is a 100% Dolcetto red meant for early drinking. Dolcetto plantings in Piedmont have fallen sharply since 2008.
rules: 1 year; release from 1 November after harvest
refs: Italian Wine Central, Dolcetto d'Alba DOC
Vertdevin, Grandi Langhe 2025 (Consorzio Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures)

Dolcetto d'Asti.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Dolcetto d'Asti.atlas_note: Dolcetto d'Asti covers 24 communes in the south of the province of Asti. It is a 100% Dolcetto red.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Dolcetto d'Asti DOC

Dolcetto di Ovada.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Dolcetto di Ovada.atlas_note: Dolcetto di Ovada covers 22 communes around Ovada in the south of the province of Alessandria. It is the young Dolcetto of the area; the aged Superiore is the separate DOCG Ovada.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Dolcetto di Ovada DOC

Fara.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Fara.atlas_note: Fara is a tiny Nebbiolo based DOC in Fara Novarese and Briona in the province of Novara. It is a blend with Vespolina and Uva Rara.
rules: at least 60% Nebbiolo; up to 40% Uva Rara and/or Vespolina

Freisa d'Asti.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Freisa d'Asti.atlas_note: Freisa d'Asti makes red wines, still or sparkling, from the Freisa grape in the province of Asti. Freisa is a relative of Nebbiolo with firm tannin.
rules: 1 year, of which 6 months in wood
refs: Italian Wine Central, Freisa d'Asti DOC

Freisa di Chieri.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Freisa di Chieri.atlas_note: Freisa di Chieri covers 13 communes of the hills around Chieri, east of Turin. It makes still and sparkling reds from Freisa.
rules: 1 year, of which 6 months in wood
refs: Italian Wine Central, Freisa di Chieri DOC

Gabiano.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Gabiano.atlas_note: Gabiano is one of the smallest DOCs of Italy, in Gabiano and Moncestino in the north of the Monferrato Casalese. It is a Barbera based red.
rules: 90 to 95% Barbera; 5 to 10% Freisa, Grignolino, Dolcetto and/or Nebbiolo
2 years, of which 18 months in wood

Grignolino d'Asti.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Grignolino d'Asti.atlas_note: Grignolino d'Asti covers 35 communes of the province of Asti. Grignolino makes a pale red with high acidity and firm tannin.
rules: at least 90% Grignolino; up to 10% Freisa
refs: Italian Wine Central, Grignolino d'Asti DOC

Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese.atlas_note: Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese covers 34 communes of the Monferrato around Casale Monferrato in the province of Alessandria. It makes pale, tannic reds and a sparkling rose from Grignolino.
rules: at least 18 months on the lees
refs: Italian Wine Central, Grignolino del Monferrato Casalese DOC

Langhe.vine_area_src: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures, as cited by Vertdevin (29 Jan 2025); reference year not stated, probably area registered in the schedario (secondary citation). Italian Wine Central gives 2,012 ha for 2021.
Langhe.atlas_note: Langhe is the umbrella DOC of the Langhe hills in the province of Cuneo, in 93 communes. It covers many varietal wines and blends, the best known being Langhe Nebbiolo. It is often used for wines declassified from Barolo or Barbaresco and for international varieties. New Langhe Nebbiolo plantings were capped from 2025.
rules: at least 85% Nebbiolo; new registrations capped at 70 ha in 2026
refs: Vertdevin, Grandi Langhe 2025 (Consorzio Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani key figures)

Lessona.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Lessona.atlas_note: Lessona is a single commune Nebbiolo DOC in the province of Biella. Its vineyards lie on acid marine sands. It is one of the most perfumed Nebbiolo wines of northern Piedmont.
rules: at least 85% Nebbiolo; up to 15% Vespolina and/or Uva Rara

Loazzolo.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed). Federdoc gives only 1.06 ha declared in 2016, so the 51 ha figure likely counts the whole Moscato area that may claim the DOC.
Loazzolo.atlas_note: Loazzolo is a single commune DOC in the province of Asti for a sweet wine from late harvested and dried Moscato Bianco. It is aged in wood.
rules: 2 years, of which 6 months in wood

Malvasia di Casorzo d'Asti / Malvasia di.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Malvasia di Casorzo d'Asti / Malvasia di.atlas_note: This DOC covers Casorzo and three nearby communes on the border between the provinces of Asti and Alessandria. It makes sweet, aromatic red, rose and sparkling wines and a passito from Malvasia Nera di Casorzo.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Malvasia di Casorzo d'Asti DOC

Malvasia di Castelnuovo Don Bosco.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Malvasia di Castelnuovo Don Bosco.atlas_note: This DOC covers six communes around Castelnuovo Don Bosco in the north of the province of Asti. It makes a sweet, aromatic red, still or sparkling, from Malvasia di Schierano.
rules: at least 85% Malvasia Nera (di Schierano or Nera Lunga); up to 15% Freisa
refs: Italian Wine Central, Malvasia di Castelnuovo Don Bosco DOC

Monferrato.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Monferrato.atlas_note: Monferrato is the umbrella DOC of the Monferrato hills in the provinces of Asti and Alessandria, in 226 communes. It covers white, rosato (Chiaretto) and red blends and varietal wines. Monferrato Nebbiolo has grown in recent years.
rules: at least 85% Cortese, from the Casalese subzone

Nebbiolo d'Alba.atlas_note: Nebbiolo d'Alba covers Nebbiolo vineyards of the Roero and parts of the Langhe around Alba, in 32 communes. It makes 100% Nebbiolo reds and sparkling wines. It is a step below Barolo and Barbaresco in ageing rules.
rules: 15 ha in 2026, 1 ha per farm (Regione Piemonte bando)

Piemonte.atlas_note: Piemonte is the regional umbrella DOC, covering the wine hills of the provinces of Alessandria, Asti and Cuneo, about 400 communes. It covers many varietal and blended wines, the largest being Piemonte Barbera, plus Moscato, Chardonnay and sparkling wines. Barbera, Moscato and Brachetto grapes from the DOCG zones can fall back on it.
rules: new registrations suspended 2025 to 2027 (Regione Piemonte DD 1053/2024)

Pinerolese.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Pinerolese.atlas_note: Pinerolese covers 34 communes around Pinerolo, south west of Turin, at the mouth of the Chisone and Pellice valleys. It makes reds from Barbera, Dolcetto and Freisa and from local grapes such as Avanà, Avarengo and Doux d'Henry.
rules: at least 60% Avanà, Avarengo, Becuet and/or Chatus; only from Perosa Argentina and Pomaretto

Rubino di Cantavenna.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Rubino di Cantavenna.atlas_note: Rubino di Cantavenna is a tiny red DOC in two communes of the Monferrato Casalese, on the hills above the Po. It is a Barbera based blend.
rules: at least 75% Barbera; up to 25% Freisa and/or Grignolino
refs: Italian Wine Central, Rubino di Cantavenna DOC

Sizzano.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Sizzano.atlas_note: Sizzano is a single commune Nebbiolo based DOC in the province of Novara, just south of Ghemme. It is a blend with Vespolina and Uva Rara.
rules: at least 60% Nebbiolo; up to 40% Uva Rara and/or Vespolina

Strevi.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Strevi.atlas_note: Strevi is a single commune DOC in the province of Alessandria for a passito from dried Moscato Bianco. It is one of the smallest DOCs of Italy.
rules: 2 years; release from 1 October of the second year after harvest

Terre Alfieri.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Terre Alfieri.atlas_note: Terre Alfieri covers 11 communes between the Roero and the Asti hills, on both sides of the Tanaro. It makes a white from Arneis and a red from Nebbiolo. It was a DOC from 2009 and became a DOCG in 2020.
rules: 1 year, of which 6 months in wood
2 years, of which 12 months in wood

Valli Ossolane.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Valli Ossolane.atlas_note: Valli Ossolane covers 17 communes of the Ossola valleys in the far north of Piedmont, near Switzerland. It makes whites mainly from Chardonnay and reds from Nebbiolo (locally Prünent), Croatina and Merlot.
refs: Italian Wine Central, Valli Ossolane DOC

Valsusa.vine_area_src: Italian Wine Central denomination page, 2021 vineyard area (secondary source; it does not say whether planted, registered or claimed)
Valsusa.atlas_note: Valsusa covers 19 communes of the Susa valley west of Turin, on mountain slopes on the route to France. It makes reds from Avanà and Becuet and a white from Baratuciat.

Verduno Pelaverga / Verduno.atlas_note: Verduno Pelaverga covers Verduno and parts of La Morra and Roddi, at the northern edge of the Barolo zone. It makes a light, peppery red from Pelaverga Piccolo.

region.vine_area_src: Planted vineyard area in the ARTEA schedario viticolo at 31 July 2024 (Regione Toscana, presentation of 3 Feb 2025). Of this, 58,079 ha (94.5%) is eligible for DOCG or DOC. ISMEA-based press material gave almost 61,000 ha in Feb 2024.
region.grape_share_note: Shares of the 61,431 ha regional vineyard, computed from the hectares per variety in the Regione Toscana 2025 presentation (ARTEA schedario, 2024). The Feb 2024 PrimAnteprima release gave Sangiovese 59%, Merlot 8%, Cabernet Sauvignon 6%, Trebbiano Toscano 4%, Vermentino 3%.
region.atlas_note: Tuscany had 61,431 ha of vineyard in 2024, held by 12,479 farms. Siena (20,789 ha) and Florence (17,130 ha) hold most of it, then Grosseto, Arezzo and Livorno. Sangiovese covers 57% of the vineyard and is the base of almost every red DOCG. The region has 11 DOCG and 41 DOC, and 94.5% of the vineyard is eligible for a DOP. Chianti and Chianti Classico together make up about 62% of the claimed DOP area.
